title: ReSOT: Re-balance Semantic ID with Optimal Transport for Generative Recommendation

problem.claim: Generative recommendation depends on effective item tokenization into discrete semantic IDs, but learning such tokenization remains challenging.

gap.claim: Existing point-wise or heuristic tokenization methods can distort relational structure because reconstruction losses insufficiently preserve item relations and collision-mitigation-driven code assignment disrupts semantic neighborhoods.

contributions.claim: ReSOT is a unified framework that re-balances semantic ID learning for generative recommendation using optimal transport.

ReSOT combines structure-aware reconstruction for aligning item-item relations with unbalanced optimal-transport soft quantization for balancing collision mitigation and semantic neighborhood preservation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on real-world datasets show that ReSOT preserves relational structure while assigning codes in a collision-aware and semantics-consistent manner.
The authors report that the code is publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Generative recommendation represents items as discrete semantic IDs in an autoregressive generation formulation.
Effective item tokenization is difficult, and existing point-wise or heuristic approaches can distort relational structure.
ReSOT addresses the distortion problem through structure-aware reconstruction and unbalanced optimal-transport soft quantization.
Experiments on real-world datasets are reported to demonstrate relational-structure preservation and collision-aware, semantics-consistent code assignment.
The authors report that the implementation is available online.

source_observation.claim: Recommendation depends on relative item similarity, while point-wise reconstruction and collision mitigation can distort item relations and semantic neighborhoods.

interpretation.claim: Representation learning for recommendation should preserve relational structure rather than optimize item-level reconstruction alone.

application.claim: When designing discrete item tokenization, evaluate and optimize both neighborhood preservation and collision behavior.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this lesson generalizes beyond the reported generative recommendation setting.

unknowns: Specific datasets, baselines, metrics, and quantitative results are not provided.
The abstract does not describe computational cost, limitations, or ablation results.
